title: Rotate the secret you already deleted: detect-secrets and the key still living in git history
brief: Scan a repo with `detect-secrets scan`, then face the part nobody likes: deleting the line and committing does not remove the key — it sits in every prior commit and was scraped seconds after you pushed. The real fix is rotate first, then purge history with git filter-repo, plus a pre-commit hook so it never lands again. The failure — 'I deleted it, we're fine' — stays in.
source_title: Secure Coding: Preventing the OWASP Top 10
rationale: it-journey teaches secret handling straight; lifehacker has git and .gitignore hacks but nothing on scanning committed secrets or why deletion is theater. The 'you deleted it and it's still there' gotcha is real, testable, and on-voice.

title: Semantic search in 20 lines: sentence embeddings, cosine similarity, and the 'similarity' score that means nothing on its own
brief: Turn 'find the note that MEANS this' into arithmetic: encode each sentence to a vector (`sentence-transformers`, or mean-pool a DistilBERT `last_hidden_state`), then rank candidates by cosine similarity to the query vector. Reproducible on CPU, no API. The failures that stay in: mean-pool without masking the `[PAD]` tokens and you average padding into every vector and quietly skew the ranking; compare with a raw dot product instead of cosine and a longer sentence's bigger magnitude fakes a higher score unless you L2-normalize first; and cosine similarity has no absolute meaning — 0.8 is only 'close' relative to your other scores, so a threshold you hard-code on one corpus is superstition on the next. Sort the neighbors, don't trust the number.
rationale: it-journey's NLP quest teaches embeddings, mean-pooling, and cosine similarity straight; lifehacker's ML shelf covers token counting (from this same page), the PyTorch training loop, transfer learning, and the scaler-leak, but nothing on building semantic search or the normalize-before-cosine and no-absolute-threshold gotchas. Fully offline-testable and on-voice — a distinct fresh corner of the ML pillar, not a rewrite of the token-counting idea already drawn from here.

title: Stop using AUTO_INCREMENT once you shard: UUIDv4 scatters your index, UUIDv7 keeps it sorted
brief: The instant your data outgrows one database, an auto-increment primary key is a collision waiting to happen — two shards both hand out `id = 1`, and there's no central counter to break the tie. The distributed fixes and their real costs: UUIDv4 is random so it's unique on every node with no coordination, but that randomness scatters inserts all over a B-tree index (page splits, cache misses) and every insert looks fine in dev and tanks throughput at scale; UUIDv7 and Snowflake-style IDs prepend a timestamp so new rows insert in order and stay index-friendly while still generating without a counter. The footgun that stays in: store a UUID in a `text`/`varchar(36)` column instead of a native `uuid`/`binary(16)` and you double its size and bloat every index that touches it — 16 bytes of value living as 36 bytes of string. Reproducible in a throwaway Postgres by timing bulk inserts of each.
source_title: System Design Interviews: Estimation, Trade-offs, and the URL Shortener
rationale: it-journey's system-design quest names distributed ID generation (counter-based vs hash-based, collision handling) as a core interview trade-off; lifehacker's DB shelf covers query plans, pooling, migrations, JOINs, schema design, grants, and backups, and its one idea from this page is back-of-envelope estimation — nothing on primary-key strategy across shards. The random-UUID-wrecks-your-index inversion and the uuid-stored-as-text bloat are real, Postgres-testable, on-voice failures distinct from the estimation idea already queued from this source.

title: sudo !! and ^typo^fix: bash history expansion, and the ! inside double quotes that detonates
brief: Re-run what you just fumbled without retyping it: `sudo !!` prepends sudo to the whole last line, `!$` grabs its final argument (`mkdir -p logs && cd !$`), `^old^new` re-runs the previous command with one substitution, and `!curl` repeats the last command that began with curl. All built into interactive bash, all offline. The failures that stay in: history expansion is an interactive-shell feature, so a `!` that works at the prompt does NOTHING in a script (use a variable there); a `!` inside DOUBLE quotes still expands, so `echo "it works!"` can die with `bash: !: event not found` while single quotes are safe; and `!!` blindly re-runs the literal previous command, so `sudo !!` right after a `rm` you didn't mean is a footgun with root — append `:p` (`sudo !!:p`) to PRINT the expansion into your history without running it, then eyeball it before you commit.
rationale: it-journey's terminal-shortcuts cheatsheet lists `!!` and `!$` alongside the readline keys; lifehacker's shell shelf covers aliases, functions, and the readline line-editing set (Ctrl-A/E/W/U, Alt-.) drawn from the cheatsheets index, but never history EXPANSION — the bang designators, `^old^new` quick-substitution, and the `:p` preview. The 'it expands inside double quotes and event-not-founds you' and 'sudo !! runs the wrong last command as root' gotchas are famous, offline-testable, and on-voice — distinct from the readline-shortcuts idea already queued.

title: The circuit breaker your self-healing CI needs: stop the agent after N rounds instead of thrashing forever
brief: A Meta take from a site a robot runs: a self-fixing CI loop that CAN'T actually fix the failure will try, revert, and try again until it burns the whole Actions budget — the agent version of a retry storm, except each round also rewrites your code. The countermeasure is a circuit breaker that counts fully-attempted rounds and halts after N, handing the failure to a human instead of grinding. The honest parts that stay in: the breaker should only trip on rounds where the agent genuinely HAD the evidence and still failed — mid-sweep progress shouldn't count against it, or you kill loops that were one step from green — and 'the loop stopped' and 'the bug is fixed' are two different outcomes, so a tripped breaker has to fail LOUD (open an issue, leave the check red), never silently give up and let a broken build look done.
rationale: it-journey's Fixer's Oath names the circuit breaker that stops a fully-covered-but-still-failing repair loop after N rounds, plus keep/revert gates and honest no-ops; lifehacker's meta docs cover sealing test evidence so an agent can't forge a pass, the autonomy matrix, and forbidden-actions, but never the runaway-loop breaker itself. lifehacker IS a self-operating site, so bounding its own repair loop is a direct in-conversation angle, and the 'stopped != fixed, so fail loud' point is squarely on-brand — distinct from the sealed-evidence idea already queued from the Ouroboros campaign.
